newsitem.title: USA: Rep. Roemer says RJR acknowledges new government evidence.
newsitem.headline: Rep. Roemer says RJR acknowledges new government evidence.

text.p: Representative Tim Roemer said on Tuesday he has learned that R.J. Reynolds Tobacco acknowledges the government has new evidence on the effect of its "Joe Camel" cigarette advertisements on children.

The Federal Trade Commission is investigating whether there is new evidence about RJR's "Joe Camel" campaign, which critics say attracts underage smokers, that would prompt it to take action against the advertising campaign.

Roemer said in an interview that based on his information, he knows that FTC investigators "have presented their new evidence to the RJR 'Joe Camel' folks, who said, 'We think this is new evidence and we need some time to respond.'"
A spokeswoman for R.J. Reynolds, a division of RJR Nabisco, noted that FTC investigations are confidential.

"It's really inappropriate for anyone to be discussing them," said Peggy Carter in Winston-Salem, N.C. "To repeat what we've said earlier, there has been no evidence that would warrant a conclusion different from that the FTC reached earlier on this question."
Carter had no comment on whether R.J. Reynolds had received any new evidence at all from the FTC.
The FTC voted in 1994, 3-2, not to take action against the "Joe Camel" campaign, but left the door open to future action.
An FTC spokeswoman had no comment on Roemer's statement.
Roemer said R.J. Reynolds may want time to assemble "a white paper on the new information and the new allegations."
"It seems that we're proceeding with the commissioners moving along toward a vote," the Indiana Democrat said. "I think that bodes well to our side."
Recently the FTC staff recommended a new examination of the issue, contending there was new evidence.
On March 26, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco issued a statement saying: "There has been no new substantive research reported since June 1994 that would change the results the FTC found then."
